transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Well, hello doctor. Thank you for seeing me. What brought me in... well, honestly, my head just feels so foggy lately. It’s like trying to think through a thick bowl of pea soup. I just keep mixing up simple things, you know? Like appointment times. I actually showed up at my hairdresser a whole week early on Tuesday. Margie—she’s been doing my hair since 1998, back when her salon was over on Elm Street before that awful fire took out the bakery next door—she just laughed, but it really embarrassed me. 

And it’s not just that, it's the exhibit dates down at the historical society where I help out, I keep getting those all backward. Plus, I can't even keep straight which volunteer I already called for the telephone tree. I ended up calling Barbara twice yesterday. She’s a lovely woman, makes a wonderful pecan pie, but her husband just had that double knee surgery so she’s been very stressed out, and I felt just terrible bothering her a second time when she's dealing with his physical therapy... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, yes. Just... my brain feels cloudy and I keep getting all these little things mixed up.
How long have you been experiencing this foggy feeling in your head and the problems with your memory?

Oh, let me think... it's been about four months now. Yes, it started right around the time the water damage pushed us into the remodel. The pipes in the guest bathroom just completely gave out right in the middle of the night. Can you imagine? Waking up at two in the morning to a puddle creeping out into the hallway! We had to rip up all that beautiful original hardwood. I was just sick about it, I always loved that wood. 

We ended up going with a laminate instead. The contractor—a very polite young man named Tommy—said it's waterproof, which I suppose is smart, but it just doesn't have the same warmth under your feet, you know? Tommy's wife just had a baby, actually, a little girl. They named her Hazel. Such a lovely, old-fashioned name, isn't it? I told him he needs to make sure to take lots of pictures because they just grow up in the blink of an eye... 

Wait, did I answer your question? I'm sorry, I get to talking about babies and I just completely lose my train of thought.

Have you noticed any other changes in how you think or process information, like trouble finding the right words when you speak, difficulty concentrating, problems planning or organizing things, or trouble with judging distances or navigating familiar places?

Well, no, I don't think so. I've always had plenty to say, so finding my words isn't a problem, and I can still plan out my grocery lists just fine. And I know my way around town perfectly! I still drive myself everywhere. I take the same route to the supermarket I have for thirty years. 

Although, speaking of the roads, they did just put in one of those new traffic circles over by the post office. Have you seen it? It is just a complete mess. My neighbor, Arthur, he went right over the curb of the center island last week in his Buick. He’s 82, bless his heart, and he insists his driving is as good as ever, but I saw him trying to read the church bulletin on Sunday and he had it held all the way out at arm's length. I told him, 'Arthur, you need to go get your eyes checked,' but you know how stubborn men can get about that sort of thing. His late wife, Martha, used to have to practically drag him to the dentist... 

Oh, my. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Getting all off track. But no, to answer your question, my navigating and my words and all that are just fine. It's really just that foggy feeling and mixing up my dates.
Have you been feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like helping out at the historical society or seeing your friends?

Well... yes, I suppose I have. It's just... things I used to absolutely love, they just sit there now and I can't make myself care about them at all. My watercolors, my tomato plants, even my line dancing group. I don't even care about watching the cardinals out back anymore. I haven't filled their feeder in weeks. 

I used to buy this special safflower seed mix from the hardware store downtown to keep the squirrels away—the store run by the Miller family? Old Mr. Miller passed away last spring, bless his heart, and his son David took over. But David, he went and changed the whole layout of the store! He put the birdseed all the way in the back corner past the plumbing supplies, which makes absolutely no sense if you ask me. People want to just grab their seed and go, they don't want to be tripping over PVC pipes and toilet valves. David’s wife is a real estate agent, she actually sold that big yellow Victorian on the corner of Maple last month, and I honestly think she’s the one giving him all these 'modern' retail ideas... 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, right. Yes, I just don't have the energy to care about my hobbies or the historical society right now.
Have you found it hard to get started on tasks or felt like there’s no point in doing things lately?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I can get started on things just fine. If something needs doing, I do it. Like the laundry, or making sure the kitchen counters are wiped down. I've always been very particular about a clean kitchen. My mother, she used to say a messy kitchen was the sign of a cluttered mind. 

She kept our kitchen spotless when I was growing up. We had this beautiful old enamel stove, white with green trim, and she would scrub it until it shone. She used to bake the most wonderful apple pies in that stove. The secret, she always said, was a little bit of lard in the crust. You just can't get that same flaky texture with butter, no matter what all these television chefs say nowadays. I saw one fellow on the cooking channel last week trying to make a pie crust with olive oil! Olive oil! Can you imagine? It just sounds dreadful. I told my friend Betty about it—she's the one who used to run the bakery on Elm Street before they turned it into that fancy coffee shop with the unpronounceable drinks. She agreed with me completely. We both said... 

Oh, dear, I'm wandering off again, aren't I? But no, I don't have trouble starting things, and I don't feel like there's no point to them. I still do what needs to be done around the house.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently—like eating much less or more than usual, or losing or gaining a significant amount of weight?

Well, yes, actually. I just haven't had much of an appetite at all lately. Most days I just pick at a piece of toast or maybe have a little cup of soup, because nothing really sounds good. I've even noticed my skirts are getting loose around the waist, and I certainly haven't been trying to lose any weight. 

I used to love making a nice roast on Sundays, with carrots and potatoes and a good gravy. My husband, Frank, God rest his soul, he would always say my gravy was the best in the county. He'd put it on everything—the meat, the potatoes, even his green beans! I used to buy my roasts from the butcher down on Main Street, Mr. Higgins. He always knew exactly which cut I wanted. But he retired a few years ago and moved down to Florida to live with his daughter. She's a dental hygienist down in Tampa, I think. Or maybe it was St. Petersburg? Anyway, the young man who took over the shop, he just doesn't trim the fat the same way Mr. Higgins did. I bought a chuck roast from him last Christmas and it was just terribly tough. I had to cook it for an extra two hours and even then, it wasn't quite right. My sister Clara came over for dinner that day, and she's always been a bit critical about my cooking, ever since we were girls. She brought this awful gelatin salad with marshmallows and carrots in it...

Oh, goodness, there I go again. But yes, to answer your question, my appetite is just gone and my clothes are definitely fitting looser.
Have you been feeling more tired or lacking in energy lately, even when you're getting enough rest?

Well, yes, I suppose I have been. It's the strangest thing, I wake up tired even after sleeping the whole night through. By the time I just wash up and make a little breakfast, I feel like I need to sit right back down in my armchair. 

That's the armchair we bought at that estate sale over in Westlake... oh, it must have been fifteen years ago now. It belonged to the mayor's mother, Mrs. Gable. She had the most beautiful house, filled with antiques. They say her husband made his fortune in textiles before the war. Anyway, we got this chair for a song because it had a tiny tear in the upholstery on the back, but I just draped a nice crocheted afghan over it. My Aunt Mildred made that afghan for our wedding. She was always crocheting something, that woman. She made these little poodle covers for spare rolls of toilet paper—do you remember those? Everyone had them in the seventies. Hers were always pink or mint green, with little rhinestone eyes. She used to buy the yarn at Woolworth's, back when they still had the lunch counter. I used to love getting a grilled cheese sandwich there with my mother... 

Oh, what were we talking about? I'm sorry, my mind just wanders. But yes, I'm just so terribly tired all the time, even doing the simplest things.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or have you felt restless or fidgety lately?

Well, yes, actually. My husband—well, before he passed, of course, but lately my son has been saying the same thing when he visits—he used to say I move like I'm wading through mud now. Just getting up from that armchair to answer the phone or sort the mail takes me such a long time. 

Speaking of the mail, the postman we have now, he's just a young thing, barely looks old enough to drive that little white truck. Not like Mr. Peterson, who delivered our mail for thirty years. Mr. Peterson knew everyone on the block by name. He'd always stop and give a little treat to the Nelson's golden retriever next door. That dog, oh, what was his name? Buster! Yes, Buster. He was such a sweet boy, but he had a terrible habit of digging up my prize petunias. I tried everything to keep him out of the flower beds—cayenne pepper, marigolds, even putting up a little wire fence, but he'd just jump right over it. The Nelsons felt awful about it, of course. Mrs. Nelson brought over a lovely pound cake to apologize once. It was a good cake, but a bit dry. I always add a dollop of sour cream to my pound cake batter, it keeps it so moist. I learned that trick from a magazine back in the sixties, I think it was Ladies' Home Journal... 

Oh, dear me, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Just talking your ear off about nothing. But yes, I just feel so slow these days, like every movement takes so much effort.
Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to go on living, or felt like you’re a burden to others?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I know my son worries about me being here all alone in this big house, but I don't feel like a burden to him. He's a good boy, my Thomas. He comes over every Sunday to mow the lawn, just like his father taught him. 

Frank was so particular about the lawn. He had this old push mower, one of those heavy metal ones, and he'd spend hours out there making sure the lines were perfectly straight. He used to say a man's lawn is his calling card to the neighborhood. We had the greenest grass on Elm Street, until the Johnsons moved in across the way. Mr. Johnson worked for a landscaping company, so he had all sorts of special fertilizers and weed killers. He even put in a little water feature, a fountain with a cherub pouring water out of a jug. I always thought it was a bit gaudy, to be honest. It attracted so many mosquitoes in the summer. We had to screen in the back porch just to be able to sit out there in the evenings. We used to sit out there and drink iced tea... I made it with fresh mint from my garden. Mint grows like a weed, you know. You have to plant it in a pot or it'll take over the whole yard. I learned that the hard way when I first started gardening. I planted a little sprig of peppermint and by the next year, it was in the rose bushes, the hydrangeas... 

Oh, listen to me rambling on about the garden. But no, to answer your question, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I'm just terribly tired and slow, that's all.
Can you tell me more about how you've been feeling emotionally lately? Have you felt sad, hopeless, or down most of the day, nearly every day?

Well, I wouldn't say sad, exactly. No, not really sad or hopeless. Just... flat, I suppose. Everything just feels a bit gray. 

Speaking of gray, I was just looking at the curtains in the living room the other day. They're this lovely dove gray silk, or at least they used to be. The sun has faded them so terribly on the side facing the street. I bought those curtains at a little boutique downtown that isn't even there anymore. It was called... oh, what was it? Madame Marguerite's, I think. Yes, Marguerite's. She was a French woman, very elegant, always wore her hair in a tight little chignon and had these beautiful silk scarves tied around her neck. She told me the silk came all the way from Lyon. I don't know if that was true, but they were certainly expensive enough! Frank nearly had a fit when he saw the credit card bill. But they hung so beautifully. They had these little weighted hems so they'd drape just right. You don't see craftsmanship like that anymore. Now everything is just bought online and comes in a plastic bag, all wrinkled and smelling like chemicals. I ordered a sweater from one of those catalogs last month, and when it arrived, it was so thin you could practically read a newspaper through it... 

But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I'm feeling hopeless or anything like that. Just... not quite myself, I guess.

Mrs. Nelson brought over a lovely pound cake to apologize once. It was a good cake, but a bit dry. I always add a dollop of sour cream to my pound cake batter, it keeps it so moist. I learned that trick from a magazine back in the sixties, I think it was Ladies' Home Journal... 

Oh, dear me, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Just talking your ear off about nothing. But yes, I just feel so slow these days, like every movement takes so much effort.

doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to go on living, or felt like you’re a burden to others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal thoughts or feelings of worthlessness/being a burden, which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I mean, I know my son worries about me being here all alone in this big house, but I don't feel like a burden to him. He's a good boy, my Thomas. He comes over every Sunday to mow the lawn, just like his father taught him. 

Frank was so particular about the lawn. He had this old push mower, one of those heavy metal ones, and he'd spend hours out there making sure the lines were perfectly straight. He used to say a man's lawn is his calling card to the neighborhood. We had the greenest grass on Elm Street, until the Johnsons moved in across the way. Mr. Johnson worked for a landscaping company, so he had all sorts of special fertilizers and weed killers. He even put in a little water feature, a fountain with a cherub pouring water out of a jug. I always thought it was a bit gaudy, to be honest. It attracted so many mosquitoes in the summer. We had to screen in the back porch just to be able to sit out there in the evenings. We used to sit out there and drink iced tea... I made it with fresh mint from my garden. Mint grows like a weed, you know. You have to plant it in a pot or it'll take over the whole yard. I learned that the hard way when I first started gardening. I planted a little sprig of peppermint and by the next year, it was in the rose bushes, the hydrangeas... 

Oh, listen to me rambling on about the garden. But no, to answer your question, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I'm just terribly tired and slow, that's all.

doctor.question: Can you tell me more about how you've been feeling emotionally lately? Have you felt sad, hopeless, or down most of the day, nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood (feeling sad, hopeless, or down), which is not listed in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't say sad, exactly. No, not really sad or hopeless. Just... flat, I suppose. Everything just feels a bit gray. 

Speaking of gray, I was just looking at the curtains in the living room the other day. They're this lovely dove gray silk, or at least they used to be. The sun has faded them so terribly on the side facing the street. I bought those curtains at a little boutique downtown that isn't even there anymore. It was called... oh, what was it? Madame Marguerite's, I think. Yes, Marguerite's. She was a French woman, very elegant, always wore her hair in a tight little chignon and had these beautiful silk scarves tied around her neck. She told me the silk came all the way from Lyon. I don't know if that was true, but they were certainly expensive enough! Frank nearly had a fit when he saw the credit card bill. But they hung so beautifully. They had these little weighted hems so they'd drape just right. You don't see craftsmanship like that anymore. Now everything is just bought online and comes in a plastic bag, all wrinkled and smelling like chemicals. I ordered a sweater from one of those catalogs last month, and when it arrived, it was so thin you could practically read a newspaper through it... 

But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I'm feeling hopeless or anything like that. Just... not quite myself, I guess.
